title: Chapter 3: Control Flow, Methods, and Decomposition
description: Turn examples and constraints into executable control flow. The chapter requires decision tables, exhaustive switch expressions, loop invariants, termination arguments, method preconditions and postconditions, overload analysis, recursion traces, and decomposition that keeps each rule testable in isolation.

lessons.title: Conditions, switch expressions, and exhaustive decisions

exercises.title: Conditions, switch expressions, and exhaustive decisions: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A shipping threshold includes exactly 10 kg. Which boundary must be tested?
choices: Only positive values not equal to 10
Values below, equal to, and above 10
hints: An inclusive threshold needs three checks, not one: test a value just below, exactly at, and just above the cutoff to see which comparison operator the rule actually uses.

lessons.title: Loops, invariants, termination, break, and continue

exercises.title: Loops, invariants, termination, break, and continue: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What is true before iteration i in an array-prefix sum?
choices: The accumulator equals the sum of the values before index i
The whole array is already summed
i is always a valid index after termination
hints: The invariant describes what has already been accumulated before index i runs, up to but not including it; trace total by hand for the first couple of iterations to see this.

lessons.title: Method contracts, parameters, return values, and side effects

exercises.title: Method contracts, parameters, return values, and side effects: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A method reassigns its int[] parameter to a new array. What changes in the caller?
choices: The caller's variable still refers to its previous array
hints: Reassigning a parameter changes only that parameter's local copy of the reference; the caller's variable still points at whatever array it referenced before the call.

lessons.title: Overloading, varargs, argument passing, and recursion

exercises.title: Overloading, varargs, argument passing, and recursion: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: When are overloaded method signatures selected?
choices: By return value desired by the user
At compile time from argument types
Only after inspecting runtime object fields
hints: Overload resolution happens at compile time from the argument's declared types; runtime object fields never enter into which method gets selected.

lessons.title: From examples and constraints to a decomposed algorithm

exercises.title: From examples and constraints to a decomposed algorithm: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why keep positiveTotal separate from console reading?
choices: The rule can be tested and reused with other input sources
It eliminates the need for validation
hints: A method that only takes an array and returns a value, with no I/O inside it, can be called from a console, a file, or a test without any changes to the rule itself.

exercises.title: Control Flow, Methods, and Decomposition: professional judgment
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A loop sometimes never finishes. What must be established?
choices: Progress toward a terminating condition on every repeating path

exercises.title: Chapter 3 implementation lab: classify
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `classify`. Return negative, zero, or positive according to the supplied integer. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Handle every int; compare with zero without negating the value.
hints: Translate "negative, zero, or positive" into two comparisons against 0, ordered so every int falls into exactly one branch.
Trace the two public examples plus the extreme boundaries Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE before submitting.

exercises.title: Inclusive loop boundary
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `10`. The loop's continuation condition `i<4` stops one iteration early and excludes 4 from the running sum, which is why the total comes out short of 1+2+3+4; preserve the demonstrated accumulation and explain why adjusting the loop's boundary, rather than hard-coding the total, restores the required sum.
hints: The requirement is the sum of 1 through 4 inclusive.
